The College Where Martin Luther King Is Problematic
This is the inevitable culmination of virtue signaling. Though it really does make for some hilarious headlines.

First off, that headline is fucking awful. There is an implicit imperative verb, "[Read about] the college where..." and then confusion.

Second, the idea of critically thinking about the King quote would be quite appropriate for a college if that is what was actually going on, but it isn't. There is no consideration of the context of the quote or of the person who said it by these protesters, this exercise is pure anti-intellectualism. Any historic figure, any event or place that has meaning associated with the problems of the past is a target for the new political correctness.
Implicit imperative verb? The headline makes complete sense as a title.

There is an implicit verb which I take to be a "call to action" imperative verb.

  • [Read about] the college where MLK is problematic

It could also be:

  • [The University of Oregon is] the college where MLK is problematic

Or perhaps:

  • The college where [students find] MLK is problematic

But that is awkward. Better:

  • The college where [students find] MLK [to be] problematic

And less clickbait-y:

  • At the University of Oregon, students find MLK to be problematic

It's a story headline, it doesn't need to be grammatically structured like a sentence. "The college where MLK is problematic" is perfectly succinct and accurately describes the article. Keep it simple, you only get so many characters to show. If you wanted to be more specific to a geography you could use "Oregon Students Find MLK Problematic". With your logic, every headline or title would require [Read about]... "[Read about... the] Three Fire [truck] Alarm At Fire [In] Downtown [Toronto]." That's not how article titles work, too long.

Of these two:

  • Oregon Students Find MLK Problematic
  • The College Where MLK Is Problematic

both contain what appears to be a verb, but in one case the verb is part of a conditional phrase (MLK is problematic). This ambiguity makes the sentence confusing to parse, you expect:

  • The college where MLK is running for student council has raised its tuition

or something similar.

Sure, we don't need an explicit verb. Here's an even more condensed version:

  • Oregon Students: MLK Problematic

"problematic" is a descriptive adjective to describe MLK, you don't need the "is". While I admire your skill and dedication to the English language, I'd wager you'd make a newspaper editor nuts to the point where he'd write your headlines for you!

Admittedly, headlines are supposed to be ambiguous, only descriptive enough to entice someone to read the rest.
